bridges.mechanism: Sustained rises in long-term U.S. yields increase federal interest costs and create domestic fiscal pressure that delays or reduces forward military deployments, arms procurements, and allied reassurance programs in the region, which Pyongyang exploits by increasing missile tests and drills.

Higher long-term yields increase the cost of capital and raise hurdle rates for capital-intensive datacenter and accelerator purchases, reducing planned procurement and build-outs of AI compute capacity.

Tighter bond-market liquidity raises transaction costs and uncertainty for leveraged financings and share-based valuations, causing acquirers and targets to delay or cancel AI M&A and strategic investments.

Acute deterioration in US bond-market liquidity raises short-term funding and trade-finance costs for tanker operators and commodity traders, causing delays or cancellations of financed voyages and a drop in shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Rapid reallocations into commodity assets (notably energy) push up oil and gas prices, increasing Russian export revenue and short-term liquidity that can be channeled into procurement, munitions consumption, and the tempo of long-range strike and drone operations.
Portfolio reallocation out of stressed US bonds into equities and growth sectors drives near-term increases in venture, private equity and public funding directed at AI startups and funds.
Net shifts of capital out of bonds into commodity allocations bid up oil futures and prompt physical traders to draw inventories or cover shorts, raising benchmark crude prices within weeks.

Changes in cross-border capital inflows alter the amount of foreign direct and portfolio investment available for US AI companies and funds, so a drop in international capital reduces AI-directed investment.

Sustained high-rate long-range strike and drone use in Ukraine prompts North Korean leadership to accelerate and publicize its own missile/rocket tests and launch activity to validate doctrines and signal deterrence.

More intensive long-range and unmanned strikes produce clearer forensic evidence of dual‑use components and supply-chain links (e.g., commercial drone parts, avionics) traceable to Chinese suppliers, prompting targeted export restrictions and customs enforcement that raise cross-border limits on relevant tech flows to China.

A sustained uptick in long-range strike intensity raises the probability of broader commodity and supply shocks and increases term premium and inflation expectations, pushing up long-term government bond yields.

A surge in long‑range and drone strikes that damages export terminals, raises the odds of further disruption, and increases insurance and risk premia for tanker routes causes immediate upward pressure on benchmark crude prices independent of an exact measured physical shortfall.

Large-scale external weapons deliveries to Ukraine spur expanded export controls, secondary-sanctions regimes and enhanced maritime/dual‑use screening that raise the prevalence and restrictiveness of trade barriers affecting routes and firms used by North Korea and its trading partners.

A sustained rise in external arms deliveries exposes procurement/financing channels and corporate intermediaries, triggering stricter national-security reviews and sanctions that slow or block cross-border M&A and strategic investments involving AI-related firms with Chinese counterparties.

Faster external arms deliveries and procurement financing redirect capital toward defense equities and away from safe‑income assets, producing net outflows from core bond allocations and a reallocation into sectors tied to military spending.

Damage to transport, energy, and communications infrastructure in or near trading/clearing hubs disrupts operational flows and dealer capacity, reducing market depth and increasing transaction costs in bond markets.

Severe damage to Black Sea export infrastructure forces crude and refined product exporters to reroute cargoes away from Ukrainian/Black Sea ports toward Gulf suppliers, increasing the number and volume of tankers transiting Middle Eastern chokepoints (e.g., Strait of Hormuz).

Degraded logistics resilience (port closures, damaged transit routes, insurance and transit delays) directly delays or cancels shipments of GPUs/accelerators and rack systems from East Asian manufacturers to cloud providers and data centers in China, reducing deployed AI compute capacity there and in aggregated cross-border deployments.

Improved logistics resilience (clearing, storage, and alternative routing) in the Russia–Ukraine theater preserves export flows and emergency stock rotations, directly reducing the risk of a measurable physical oil supply shortfall in global markets.

Rising reciprocal escalation in the Russia–Ukraine theater raises great-power threat perceptions and produces more assertive military and diplomatic postures by Russia, China and the United States in other theaters, increasing strategic rivalry around the Korean Peninsula.

A spike in escalation (high-profile uses of force and reciprocal provocations) rapidly elevates US/EU threat perceptions and domestic political pressure, producing fast-moving executive actions and regulatory expansions (export controls, investment screening, sanctions) that increase trade and tech-transfer barriers vis-à-vis China.

Rising escalation pressure (reciprocal strikes, provocative acts) directly raises short-term risk premia and urgency in hedging demand, producing immediate spikes in realized and implied volatility across bond and related markets.

Rising escalation pressure in the Russia–Ukraine war drives Washington and NATO to reallocate naval and air deterrent assets to Europe and signals heightened great-power competition, which reduces perceived US capacity/deterrence in the Gulf and encourages Iranian forces and proxies to probe or escalate, raising regional escalation risk.

Stronger targeted sanctions on Iranian procurement and export networks disrupt Iran's ability to produce and legally ship drones and munitions, reducing one external source of weapons and components available to Russia.

U.S. escalation of sanctions and secondary-sanctions authorities against Iranian entities leads Commerce/Treasury to broaden export controls and licensing requirements (including tighter end‑user/end‑use checks), which raises de facto barriers on cross‑border movement of AI‑related goods and tech involving Chinese intermediaries.

Tighter sanctions raise compliance costs and counterparty risk, prompting banks and primary dealers to reduce interdealer inventory and repo/market-making activity in affected instruments, directly reducing bond-market liquidity.

Sustained higher crude prices materially raise Russian hydrocarbon revenues and budgetary headroom, enabling faster procurement/consumption of munitions and fuel that support a higher tempo of long-range strike and drone campaigns.

Sharp increases in crude/oil prices raise electricity and cooling costs for data centers and shipping/installation costs for hardware, reducing the economic incentive to commission new large‑scale AI compute deployments and delaying capacity expansions.

A sustained rise in crude prices lifts near-term inflation and inflation expectations and forces investors to demand higher nominal compensation on long-dated government bonds, pushing long-term yields up.

A spike in Gulf escalation draws U.S. naval and air assets into the Middle East, reducing forward-deployed deterrence in East Asia and creating a perceived window that North Korea exploits with more frequent missile tests and drills.

Heightened kinetic/coercive activity in the Gulf draws U.S. and allied command attention and forces into the region and degrades deterrence signaling in Europe, which Russia exploits to intensify reciprocal probing and provocative operations against Ukraine.

Heightened Gulf conflict risk increases investor risk aversion toward geopolitically exposed markets and supply chains, prompting reallocations of private and sovereign capital into domestic/ally AI projects and defense‑adjacent AI startups perceived as safer.
Higher risk of kinetic or coercive escalation increases uncertainty and rapid repricing of geopolitical risk premia, producing sharp swings in bond prices and implied/realized volatility.

Growth in accessible AI compute (accelerators, cloud cycles) speeds development of autonomy, swarm coordination and target‑recognition software that can be integrated into loitering munitions and ISR-to-shooter chains, enabling higher-frequency and more distributed strike operations.

A surge in capital directed to AI projects draws funds away from traditional fixed-income allocations (direct private placements, IPOs and equity rounds), producing measurable net reallocations out of bonds into AI-related equities and private assets.

An increase in M&A deal flow raises immediate corporate financing needs (debt-financed transactions and bridge facilities) which can heighten issuance and pull dealer balance-sheet capacity toward corporate credit, reducing demand for long-duration government bonds and pushing long-term yields up.

Rising M&A and strategic investment by Chinese firms into shipping, trading and logistics intermediaries creates new channels for Iranian oil and sanctionable activity, prompting U.S. authorities to broaden or intensify secondary sanctions against facilitators.

Faster, larger-scale deployment of operational AI models (targeting aids, automated engagement support) lowers human decision latencies and increases the pace of kinetic actions and near‑threshold incidents, raising reciprocal targeting and political pressure toward escalation.

New or tightened US-China AI export controls and trade restrictions provoke diplomatic reprisals, public signaling and reciprocal measures that directly escalate strategic rivalry and tension in the Korean Peninsula security environment.

US-imposed cross-border AI trade controls put pressure on South Korea and Japan to align licensing, screening and export-control policies, producing more near-term diplomatic coordination and policy cohesion among those allies.

Tighter US–China cross-border export controls and trade barriers choke off shipments of semiconductors, inertial/GNSS components and other dual‑use parts used by third‑party suppliers and Russian assemblers, directly reducing the tempo of externally sourced weapons and munitions arriving into the Russia–Ukraine theater.

Tighter cross-border tech/trade restrictions trigger immediate reductions in foreign investors' ability and willingness to hold domestic bonds (forced sales, reduced new purchases, and slower repatriation arrangements), producing measurable net outflows of international capital into/out of the bond market.

Higher cross-border restrictions reduce participation by foreign dealers and repo counterparties and raise compliance/frictional costs for cross-border trading, which directly thins interdealer depth and widens bid-offer spreads in the bond market.

Tighter US-China technology/trade restrictions incentivize China to deepen security, naval and arms cooperation with Iran (to secure energy and strategic leverage), which materially emboldens Iranian operational postures and raises the probability of kinetic incidents in the Gulf.

A sharp rise in North Korean nuclear-related tension forces Western suppliers and logistics partners to reassign diplomatic bandwidth, transport capacity and inspection resources to Indo‑Pacific contingencies, slowing approvals and physical deliveries of Western-supplied arms into the Russia–Ukraine theatre.

A North Korean nuclear escalation raises US and allied threat perceptions, prompting rapid targeted export controls, visa curbs and tighter licensing that directly increase cross-border barriers for AI-related goods, services and talent.

Heightened regional strategic rivalry drives global risk-off flows into US Treasuries and compresses the term premium as investors buy long-dated government paper, mechanically lowering long-term yields.
A rapid rise in DPRK nuclear-related strategic tensions increases market risk premia and short-term hedging demand, lifting benchmark crude prices even without direct supply disruptions in the Gulf.

A sustained uptick in North Korean missile tests and munitions production increases DPRK surplus stocks and political leverage, enabling faster, larger transfers of artillery, rockets and munitions to Russia for use in Ukraine.

A spike in missile tests and regional military operations creates immediate operational demand for AI-enabled ISR, warning and targeting systems, pushing defense contractors and partners to accelerate production deployments of new models.

Spikes in missile tests, live-fire drills or near-shore naval maneuvers cause sudden repricing of geopolitical risk and prompt rapid hedging and position-squaring in Treasury futures and options, creating sharp increases in realized and implied fixed-income volatility.

Intense or unpredictable military operations increase counterparty and settlement risk, leading primary dealers and market makers to widen bid-ask spreads and reduce inventories, which materially reduces on-the-run Treasury market depth and turnover.

A surge in North Korean missile tests and exercises forces U.S. and allied naval/air assets to redeploy toward Northeast Asia, creating a temporary deterrence gap in the Gulf that raises the probability of kinetic or coercive escalation involving U.S.-Iranian actors and proxies.

Greater diplomatic and policy coordination among the US and regional allies leads to joint investment-screening and coordinated blocking of transactions involving Chinese-linked AI firms, reducing cross-border M&A volume.

An uptick in export controls and investment restrictions tied to North Korea-related risk raises compliance costs and political risk, diverting international private and strategic capital away from cross-border AI ventures toward domestic or allied projects.

nodes.label: US Treasury Bond Intervention vs. a Fracturing Bond Market
Long-term bond yields
nodes.description: Measures prevailing nominal yields on long-dated government bonds across the relevant maturity curve.

nodes.label: Term premium
nodes.description: Measures the additional yield investors require to hold longer-duration bonds versus the expected path of short rates.

nodes.label: Real long-term yield
nodes.description: Measures inflation-adjusted yield on long-dated government bonds, reflecting real return expectations.

nodes.label: Market liquidity
nodes.description: Measures the ease, depth and cost of executing transactions in the bond market (e.g., spreads, market depth, turnover).

nodes.label: Market-making capacity
nodes.description: Measures aggregate ability of liquidity providers to quote two-sided prices and absorb inventory in the bond market.

nodes.label: Government debt issuance
nodes.description: Measures the rate, size and cadence of new government debt being introduced into the market.

nodes.label: Secondary market buyback activity
nodes.description: Measures the pace and volume of government purchases of outstanding securities in secondary markets.

nodes.label: Monetary policy stance
nodes.description: Measures the degree of monetary policy tightness or looseness implied by policy rates and expected future policy path.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Measures market and investor expectations for future inflation over key horizons.

nodes.label: Policy credibility
nodes.description: Measures market confidence that fiscal and monetary authorities will achieve their stated objectives without destabilizing trade-offs.

nodes.label: Investor risk appetite
nodes.description: Measures investors' willingness to hold higher-risk assets relative to safe assets at a given price.

nodes.label: Asset reallocation flows
nodes.description: Measures net shifts of capital between major asset classes (e.g., bonds, equities, commodities, crypto) over time.

nodes.label: Safe-haven demand
nodes.description: Measures net flow and price pressure into traditionally defensive assets during episodes of market stress or risk aversion.

nodes.label: Dollar exchange value
nodes.description: Measures the currency's value against a broad basket of other currencies, capturing FX-driven valuation effects.

nodes.label: Market volatility
nodes.description: Measures realized and implied short-term price variability across fixed income and related financial markets.

nodes.label: Cross-border capital flows
nodes.description: Measures net international capital movements into and out of domestic bond and broader financial markets.

nodes.label: Escalating Russia–Ukraine war: strikes, air-defence shortages, global spillovers
Strike campaign intensity
nodes.description: The aggregate rate and scale of long-range and unmanned strike operations (missile, drone, air) over time.

nodes.label: Air‑defense availability
nodes.description: The operational inventory and readiness of active air‑defense systems and intercept capacity.

nodes.label: External arms supply rate
nodes.description: The tempo at which external military equipment and munitions are delivered into the conflict system.

nodes.label: Critical infrastructure damage
nodes.description: The accumulated physical degradation or loss of key economic and logistics infrastructure (energy, transport, storage).

nodes.label: Energy market disruption
nodes.description: The degree of disturbance in energy production, transport, pricing and supply chains affecting markets beyond the conflict zone.

nodes.label: Food supply disruption
nodes.description: The extent to which agricultural production, storage and export channels are impaired, altering food availability and prices.

nodes.label: Logistics resilience
nodes.description: The capacity of military and commercial logistics networks to sustain supply flows under attack and disruption.

nodes.label: Civilian casualty rate
nodes.description: The ongoing rate of non‑combatant deaths and injuries resulting from military operations and strikes.

nodes.label: Displacement level
nodes.description: The cumulative number of people uprooted or relocated due to insecurity and infrastructure loss.

nodes.label: Political leadership stability
nodes.description: The perceived and operational stability of executive and strategic political leadership affecting decision continuity.

nodes.label: Escalation pressure
nodes.description: The tendency for conflict dynamics to intensify, measured by reciprocal targeting, provocative actions and triggers for broader use of force.

nodes.label: Air‑defense replenishment rate
nodes.description: The rate at which air‑defense systems and associated munitions are procured, manufactured, transferred and fielded to restore intercept capacity.

nodes.label: Command and control status
nodes.description: The integrity and functionality of military command, control and communications networks enabling coordinated operations.

nodes.label: Trade and logistics disruption
nodes.description: The degree to which international trade routes, ports and freight networks are impaired, delaying or rerouting commercial flows.

nodes.label: International support sentiment
nodes.description: The prevailing attitudes and willingness among external audiences and decision makers to provide diplomatic, material or political support.

nodes.label: Cumulative economic cost
nodes.description: The aggregated economic burden from direct damages, lost output and market disruption attributable to the conflict over time.

nodes.label: Sustained Russian missile and drone assaults
Ukraine attacks Russian energy and logistics sites
Depletion of Patriot munitions / launcher shortages
Ousted Ukrainian defence minister's US funding trip
US economic pressure on Iran driving energy-market disruption
Sanctions intensity
nodes.description: The breadth and severity of economic restrictions and trade/financial measures applied against the target economy.

nodes.label: Regional naval presence
nodes.description: The aggregate level of deployed military maritime assets operating in or near the maritime chokepoint and adjacent waters.

nodes.label: Chokepoint transit volume
nodes.description: The rate of commercial oil and gas tanker transits through the maritime chokepoint measured as cargo volume or ship passages per unit time.

nodes.label: Perceived navigation risk
nodes.description: Market and operator perceptions of the safety and reliability of maritime passage through the chokepoint, including threat likelihood estimates.

nodes.label: Physical oil supply shortfall
nodes.description: The net deficit between global oil demand and physically available, deliverable crude supplies attributable to disruptions or restraints.

nodes.label: Crude oil price level
nodes.description: The prevailing market price of benchmark crude oil reflecting current supply-demand balance and risk premia.

nodes.label: Natural gas price level
nodes.description: The prevailing market price of natural gas in affected markets, reflecting supply availability and infrastructure constraints.

nodes.label: Third‑party purchase rate
nodes.description: The rate at which external buyers acquire oil or gas from the targeted exporter through formal or informal channels.

nodes.label: Sanction evasion activity
nodes.description: The intensity and frequency of economic workarounds, illicit trade, re‑routing and financial obfuscation aimed at circumventing sanctions.

nodes.label: Tanker avoidance rate
nodes.description: The proportion of tankers and shipping firms choosing to reroute, delay or refuse transits through the chokepoint due to perceived hazards or restrictions.

nodes.label: Alternative route capacity
nodes.description: The available throughput capacity of non‑chokepoint transport options, storage facilities and pipeline routes that can substitute for disrupted shipping.

nodes.label: Refinery utilization
nodes.description: The operational throughput level of refining infrastructure in relevant markets, measured as percent of technical capacity in use.

nodes.label: Strategic reserve drawdown
nodes.description: The rate at which strategic petroleum or gas reserves are being released and supplied to markets to alleviate shortages.

nodes.label: Market volatility premium
nodes.description: The risk premium and price volatility in energy and related financial markets reflecting uncertainty about supply disruptions and policy actions.

nodes.label: Diplomatic coordination level
nodes.description: The degree of alignment and cooperative action among external actors on trade, sanctions, and security measures related to the crisis.

nodes.label: Regional escalation risk
nodes.description: The assessed likelihood and intensity of kinetic or coercive escalation in the region that could further disrupt energy flows.

nodes.label: Iran allows limited Iraqi tanker passages
Iran retaliatory threats or limited actions
AI boom reshaping capital, chips, data centers and markets
AI compute capacity
nodes.description: Total deployed compute resources optimized for AI workloads (accelerators, servers and effective FLOPS) available to run models and training.

nodes.label: Compute utilization rate
nodes.description: Proportion of available AI compute capacity actively used for training, inference and development tasks at a given time.

nodes.label: Memory supply capacity
nodes.description: Sustained production and inventory volume of memory components suitable for AI servers and accelerators.

nodes.label: Memory price level
nodes.description: Market-average price per unit of memory used in AI infrastructure, measured on a continuous scale.

nodes.label: Data-center capacity
nodes.description: Physical and power-constrained capacity available in data centers for hosting AI workloads (rack-space, power, cooling).

nodes.label: Data-center price level
nodes.description: Average market cost of provisioning data-center services for AI workloads (colocation, power, network) per unit of capacity.

nodes.label: Capital flow to AI
nodes.description: Rate at which investment capital (public, private and strategic) is being allocated to AI-related assets and projects.

nodes.label: Corporate liquidity pool
nodes.description: Aggregate available liquid financial resources within corporate entities that can be deployed for investment, buybacks or acquisitions.

nodes.label: Capital return rate
nodes.description: Rate of corporate distributions to owners such as buybacks and dividend payouts relative to available capital.

nodes.label: M&A deal flow
nodes.description: Velocity and monetary volume of mergers, acquisitions and strategic investments targeting AI-related businesses and capabilities.

nodes.label: Talent mobility rate
nodes.description: Rate at which skilled AI personnel move between organizations and sectors, including hiring, turnover and cross-border moves.

nodes.label: Model deployment rate
nodes.description: Frequency and scale at which new AI models and large updates are deployed into production environments.

nodes.label: Investor sentiment toward AI assets
nodes.description: Aggregate market perception and confidence regarding the future returns and risks of AI-related financial assets.

nodes.label: Supply-chain constraint level
nodes.description: Degree of bottlenecks and lead-time risk across upstream supply chains for components and materials for AI infrastructure.

nodes.label: Regulatory scrutiny level
nodes.description: Intensity of policy, regulatory and compliance pressure focused on AI technologies, data practices and infrastructure.

nodes.label: Cross-border restriction level
nodes.description: Extent of trade, investment and technology-transfer barriers affecting the international movement of AI-related goods, services and talent.

nodes.label: Ongoing price cuts among frontier model providers
China eases limits on Nvidia H200 chips
AI server price hikes roll out to customers
Geopolitical tension
nodes.description: Degree of strategic rivalry and adversarial posture among major state actors in the region.

nodes.label: Military activity intensity
nodes.description: Frequency, scale and geographic proximity of military operations, drills, missile tests and transits.

nodes.label: Alliance and alignment cohesion
nodes.description: Level of diplomatic coordination, policy alignment and cooperative interoperability among partner states.

nodes.label: Defense spending trend
nodes.description: Rate of change in government military expenditures across the regional system.

nodes.label: Economic integration level
nodes.description: Degree of cross-border trade, investment, and production interdependence among economies in the region.

nodes.label: Trade barrier intensity
nodes.description: Prevalence and restrictiveness of tariffs, export controls, investment screening and related trade policy measures.

nodes.label: Cross-border capital flows
nodes.description: Volume, direction and short-term volatility of international portfolio flows, FDI and other capital movements.

nodes.label: Corporate financial stress
nodes.description: Prevalence of solvency and liquidity pressures, default risk and distress among large corporate borrowers and issuers.

nodes.label: Market volatility
nodes.description: Level of price and liquidity volatility across equity, bond and currency markets in the region.

nodes.label: Supply chain disruption level
nodes.description: Extent of interruptions, rerouting, delays and reliability problems in critical supply chains and logistics networks.

nodes.label: Technological competition intensity
nodes.description: Degree of competition, restrictions and strategic rivalry in critical technologies and industrial capabilities.

nodes.label: Regulatory and judicial enforcement
nodes.description: Frequency, scope and severity of regulatory actions, investigations and court rulings affecting economic and security-related activities.

nodes.label: Public sentiment toward external actors
nodes.description: Aggregate popular attitudes, social support or hostility toward foreign rival actors and external partners.

nodes.label: Domestic political polarization
nodes.description: Degree of partisan and societal polarization over foreign policy, economic and security choices within societies.

nodes.label: Cross-border legal risk
nodes.description: Probability and expected magnitude of litigation, asset freezes, bankruptcy adjudication and legal restrictions on cross-border transactions.

nodes.label: Information and disinformation flow
nodes.description: Rate, reach and targeting of media narratives, strategic communications and disinformation that shape domestic and international perceptions.
